fields.title: The Letter to the Hebrews
fields.subtitle: Pros Hebraious, “To the Hebrews”
fields.description: A sermon sent as a letter, to believers who had once stood firm under persecution and were now tired and drifting, and the fullest portrait anywhere in the Bible of Jesus as priest: “Long ago God spoke to the ancestors through the prophets … But at the end of these days he has spoken to us through the Son.” The Son is the radiance of God’s glory, higher than the angels, faithful over God’s house as Moses was faithful in it; a high priest of the order of Melchizedek, who has passed through the heavens and entered the true sanctuary once for all with his own blood, and lives forever to plead for those who come to God through him. Then the great roll call of faith, from Abel to the prophets; the race run with eyes on Jesus; Mount Zion in place of Sinai; and a call to go out to him outside the camp. Its author is unknown, and its warnings are among the most searching in Scripture. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Hebrews?
qa.answer: The nineteenth book of the New Testament, written to Christians, very likely Jewish believers in Jesus, who had been through persecution and were tempted to drift away or turn back. Its author calls it a “message of encouragement” (13:22), and it reads like a sermon. It shows from the Old Testament that Jesus, God’s Son, is greater than the angels, than Moses and than the priests of Aaron’s line, that his single sacrifice has done what the old sacrifices could not, and that his people should therefore draw near to God, hold on to their hope and run with endurance.

qa.question: Who wrote Hebrews, and when?
qa.answer: No one knows. The letter names no author, and the early church already disagreed: Christians in the East counted it among Paul’s letters, though Clement of Alexandria and Origen saw that its style was not Paul’s, and Origen concluded that only God knows who wrote it. Tertullian named Barnabas; Luther suggested Apollos; others have proposed Luke, Silas or Priscilla. It was written before about AD 96, when Clement of Rome echoes it, and many scholars date it before AD 70, since it speaks of the priests’ service as still going on and never mentions the temple’s destruction.

qa.question: Who was Melchizedek, and why does Hebrews compare Jesus to him?
qa.answer: Melchizedek was the king of Salem and “priest of God Most High” who blessed Abraham and received a tenth from him in Genesis 14:18–20. Psalm 110:4 says of David’s Lord, “You are a priest forever, of the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews uses the two passages to show how Jesus, who came from the tribe of Judah and not Levi, can be a priest, and why his priesthood is greater: it rests on an oath of God and on “the power of a life that cannot be destroyed”, and it never passes to another (7:16, 24).

qa.question: What does Hebrews 6:4–6 mean about falling away?
qa.answer: The passage warns that for those who have shared in God’s gifts and then fall away, it is impossible to be brought back to repentance. Christians read it in more than one way. Many in the Reformed tradition hold that it describes people who tasted God’s gifts without true saving faith, or that the warning is one of the means by which God keeps his people; in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions it shows that genuine believers can turn away for good. All agree that the author means it seriously, and that he goes straight on to say he is confident of better things for his readers (6:9).

qa.question: What is the “cloud of witnesses” in Hebrews?
qa.answer: The men and women of faith listed in chapter 11, from Abel, Enoch and Noah to Abraham and Sarah, Moses, Rahab, the judges, David and the prophets, who trusted God’s promises without yet receiving them. In 12:1–2 the author pictures them all around believers like the crowd in a stadium, and urges his readers to throw off every burden and run their own race with endurance, keeping their eyes on Jesus, who leads the way in faith and brings it to perfection.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Long ago God spoke to the ancestors through the prophets, in many separate portions and by many different means. But at the end of these days he has spoken to us through the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things and through whom he also made the ages.

— Hebrews 1:1–2

Hebrews begins like no other letter in the New Testament. There is no greeting and no sender’s name, no “grace and peace”. It opens instead with one long, carefully balanced sentence, some of the finest Greek in the New Testament, about a God who speaks. Long ago he spoke through the prophets, in pieces and in many ways. Now, at the last, he has spoken through a Son.

Everything that follows unfolds that sentence. The Son is greater than the angels, greater than Moses, greater than the priests of Aaron’s line. His one sacrifice does what the endless sacrifices of the old covenant could only point toward. And because God has spoken so fully and so finally, those who have heard him dare not drift away.

That last point is why the book was written. Hebrews is not a treatise for scholars. Its author calls it “this message of encouragement” (13:22), and it reads like a sermon sent by post to a congregation that was tired. They had stood firm once, under real persecution. Now some had stopped meeting, and some were thinking of turning back. Into that weariness the author pours the fullest portrait of Jesus as priest anywhere in the Bible, and a call to keep running.

Who wrote it, and to whom?

No one knows who wrote Hebrews, and the early church knew that it did not know. The letter names no author. He was not one of the first eyewitnesses: the message of salvation, he says, was “made certain to us by those who had listened to him” (2:3). He knew Timothy (13:23).

In the East the letter was counted among Paul’s from early on. The oldest surviving collection of Paul’s letters, a papyrus copied around AD 200, places it straight after Romans. Clement of Alexandria thought Paul had written it in Hebrew and Luke had put it into Greek. Origen thought the ideas were Paul’s and the wording someone else’s, and concluded, in a line Eusebius preserved, that who wrote the letter, in truth, God knows. In the West, Tertullian named Barnabas, and the church at Rome was slow to count the letter as Paul’s at all. Luther later guessed Apollos, the learned Alexandrian Jew of Acts 18:24; others have suggested Luke, Silas, or Priscilla. Most scholars today agree that the style and the shape of the argument are not Paul’s. The church, East and West, received the letter as Scripture all the same.

The title “To the Hebrews” was attached early, but not by the author. Still, it fits. The whole argument moves through Israel’s Scriptures, its priesthood, its tabernacle and its Day of Atonement, and it assumes readers who know them well, very likely Jewish believers in Jesus who were tempted to fall back on the familiar ways they had left. “Those from Italy send you their greetings” (13:24) may mean the author was writing from Italy, or that Italians away from home were greeting their friends there.

As for the date, Clement of Rome echoes Hebrews in a letter written around AD 96, so it is older than that. Many think it was written before the temple fell in AD 70. The author speaks of the priests’ service as something still going on (8:4, 10:1–2), and he never mentions the temple’s destruction, which would have made his argument for him. Others place it a decade or two later. Either way, its readers had once “endured a hard contest of suffering” (10:32). Now they were drifting.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapters 1–4: the Son who speaks. Higher than the angels, faithful over God’s house as Moses was faithful in it, and the one through whom God’s promised rest is still open, “Today”.
  • Chapters 5–10:18: the great high priest. A priest of the order of Melchizedek, mediator of a new covenant, who has entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, once for all.
  • Chapters 10:19–13:25: so let us draw near, and hold on. Faith in the long roll call of chapter 11, endurance in the race of chapter 12, and love in the ordinary life of chapter 13.

Woven through the whole are five warnings, each searching (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; 5:11–6:12; 10:26–39; 12:14–29). Hebrews never lets teaching stand on its own. Every unveiling of who Jesus is ends in a “so”: so pay attention, so do not harden your hearts, so let us approach.

God has spoken in a Son

The opening sentence does not stop with the Son as God’s last word. It goes on to say who he is:

The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact stamp of his being, and he bears all things along by his word of power. Having made cleansing for sins through himself, he took his seat at the right hand of the Majesty on high. So he has become far better than the angels, as far as the name that is his by inheritance excels theirs.

— Hebrews 1:3–4

Radiance and stamp: the light that streams from the sun, and the image pressed by a seal into wax. The Son is not a reflection of God at a distance; he shows exactly what God is. Then, in seven quotations from Israel’s Scriptures, most of them from the Psalms, the author sets the Son above the angels. To which angel did God ever say, “You are my Son”? Of which angel did he say, “Your throne, O God, lasts forever and ever”?

The first warning follows at once. If the law given through angels carried its penalties, “how will we escape if we pay no attention to a salvation as great as this?” The danger Hebrews fears is not open rebellion so much as drift.

Made like his brothers and sisters

Psalm 8 marvels that God should crown human beings with glory and put all things under their feet. “But as it is,” the author admits, “we do not yet see all things put under him.” Then: “But Jesus we do see.” It is the first time the letter uses his name, and it comes at the place where the human story has fallen short.

The Son who is the radiance of God’s glory shared “a common life of flesh and blood”, so that by his death he might break the devil’s power and set free those whom the fear of death had kept enslaved all their lives. He is “not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters.” And this is the point where the letter’s great theme first appears:

That is why it was necessary for him to become like his brothers and sisters in every way, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in all that has to do with God, making atonement for the sins of the people. Having suffered himself in being tested, he is able to come to the aid of those who are being tested.

— Hebrews 2:17–18

Today, if you hear his voice

Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant; Christ is faithful over it as the Son. But the house is a people, “and we are that house, if we keep hold of our confidence”. To show what is at stake, the author turns to Psalm 95 and the generation that came out of Egypt and never reached the promised land. What kept them out was not a lack of evidence but a lack of trust: “it was unbelief that kept them from entering.”

The psalm says “Today”, and the author seizes on the word. David wrote it long after Joshua had led Israel into Canaan, so the true rest cannot have been Canaan. “So a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God’s people.” The door stands open, but only today, and so believers are to “encourage one another day by day, while there is still a ‘Today,’” before sin can harden them.

Then comes one of the letter’s most famous sentences, about the word that has been speaking all along, which “has a keener edge than any two-edged sword” and weighs “the thoughts and purposes of the heart.” No one can hide from it. But the passage turns straight from exposure to welcome:

For the high priest we have is not one who cannot share the feeling of our weaknesses; he has been put to the test in every way, as we are, but without sinning. So let us, with confidence, approach the throne of grace, to receive mercy and to find grace that brings help just when we need it.

— Hebrews 4:15–16

A priest like Melchizedek

No high priest takes the honour for himself; God calls him, and so with Christ. Here the author offers a glimpse of Jesus at prayer, most likely in Gethsemane, that no other letter in the New Testament gives: in the days of his flesh Jesus offered up prayers and pleas, “crying aloud and weeping”, and though he was a Son, “he learned obedience by the things he suffered.”

But Jesus was from the tribe of Judah, not Levi. How can he be a priest? The answer lies in Psalm 110, the psalm the New Testament quotes more than any other, where God says to David’s Lord, “You are a priest forever, of the order of Melchizedek.” Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14 for three verses, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, and then vanishes. The author reads the silence of Genesis about his parents, his birth and his death as a picture of a priesthood that has no beginning and no end. Abraham, Levi’s ancestor, gave him a tenth and received his blessing, so a priest of his order is greater than any of Aaron’s. Jesus has become one “by the power of a life that cannot be destroyed.”

The Levitical priests died one after another. This one does not:

For this reason he is able to save completely those who approach God through him, since he is always alive to plead on their behalf.

— Hebrews 7:25

The hardest warning

Before that argument, the author stops himself. His readers have become “sluggish listeners”; they should be teachers by now, and still need milk. He urges them on to maturity, and then writes the passage that has troubled more readers than any other in the letter: for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the gift from heaven and shared in the Holy Spirit, and then have fallen away, “It is impossible for them to be brought back again to repentance” (6:4–6).

Christians have read this in more than one way. In the Reformed tradition, many hold that those described had tasted God’s gifts without true saving faith, or that the warning is one of the very means by which God keeps his people from falling. In the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, it shows that real believers can turn away for good. Every reading should notice what the author does next: “Yet about you, dear friends, we are confident of better things” (6:9). The warning is meant to keep them, and the chapter ends with an anchor:

This hope is ours as an anchor for the soul, one that holds safe and firm and reaches into the inner place behind the curtain. There Jesus entered ahead of us and for our sake, as a forerunner, having become a high priest forever, of the order of Melchizedek.

— Hebrews 6:19–20

A better covenant, a single sacrifice

“Here is the heart of what we are saying” (8:1). Our high priest serves in the true tabernacle, of which the earthly one was only “a copy and shadow”. He is mediator of a better covenant, the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31. The author quotes the whole promise, the longest quotation of the Old Testament anywhere in the New, and its last line is the one he cares most about: “For I will show mercy to their wrongdoing, and their sins I will never again call to mind.”

Chapter 9 walks through the tabernacle and the Day of Atonement, when once a year the high priest went alone behind the curtain with blood. That yearly return was itself the proof that the work was never finished. Christ has entered not a sanctuary made by hands but “heaven itself”, not with the blood of goats and calves but with his own, and not over and over but once:

But Christ came as high priest of the good things that have now come. Through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, one not made by hands and not belonging to this creation, and by means not of the blood of goats and calves but of his own blood, he entered the sanctuary once for all and obtained an eternal redemption.

— Hebrews 9:11–12

“Every priest stands at his duties day after day,” the author writes. But “This priest, though, offered a single sacrifice for sins, good for all time, and then sat down at the right hand of God.” The work is done.

Draw near, hold on

At 10:19 the letter turns from what Christ has done to what his people may now do. Since the way into God’s presence is open, “let us approach”, “Let us cling to the confession of our hope”, and let us not walk away from our own gatherings, “as some have made it their practice”. Then comes the fourth warning, as severe as the third, “Falling into the hands of the living God is a terrifying thing”, and again the turn to encouragement. Remember the early days, he says, when you lost your goods and took it with joy. “What you need is endurance.”

By faith

Then the great chapter. It opens with a definition:

Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for, the proof of realities we do not see.

— Hebrews 11:1

And it goes on with a procession. By faith Abel, Enoch and Noah; by faith Abraham, who set out “without knowing where he was headed”, and Sarah, and Isaac, Jacob and Joseph; by faith Moses, and Israel at the Red Sea, and the walls of Jericho, and Rahab. Then the pace quickens, through judges, kings and prophets, to those who shut the mouths of lions and those who were sawn in two. “The world did not deserve such people.”

What they share is not success. Many of them “did not receive what was promised, but they saw it from far off and welcomed it”, and they called themselves “foreigners and passing visitors on the earth.” Faith, in Hebrews, is trusting God about what has not happened yet, and living now as if his promises were already solid ground. And the chapter ends with a surprise: none of them has yet been made perfect. They are waiting for us.

The race and the mountain

So chapter 12 pictures them filling the stands of a stadium:

So then, since we too have so vast a cloud of witnesses all around us, let us strip off every burden, and the sin that wraps itself around us so readily, and let us run the race laid out ahead of us, and run it with endurance. Let us keep our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer who leads the way in faith and brings it to perfection. For the sake of the joy that lay ahead of him, he endured a cross and counted its shame as nothing, and he has taken his seat at the right hand of God’s throne.

— Hebrews 12:1–2

The hardships of the race, the author says, are a Father’s discipline, the training every true child receives. Then he sets two mountains side by side. Israel came to Sinai, to fire and darkness and a voice so terrible that they begged it to stop. Believers have come to Mount Zion, “the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem”, to myriads of angels in festival gathering, to Jesus, and to his sprinkled blood, “which says something better than Abel said.” Abel’s blood cried out for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks pardon. The privilege is greater, and so is the responsibility: “For our God really is a consuming fire.”

Outside the camp

The last chapter is plain and practical. Keep loving one another. Open your homes to strangers, for “some people have had angels as their guests and never knew it.” Remember prisoners. Honour marriage. Be content, for God has said, “I will not ever let you go, and I will never, never abandon you.”

And then one last image from the Day of Atonement. The bodies of the sacrificed animals were burned outside the camp, and Jesus too “suffered outside the gate”. So, says the author, “let us go out to him, outside the camp, and share the insults heaped on him.” For readers tempted to retreat into safety, it is the letter’s final appeal. The security they long for is not behind them. “There is no city here that remains for us; the city we are looking for is the one still to come.”

How to read Hebrews

Read it aloud, at one sitting if you can, as its first hearers did. You will hear its rhythm: each stretch of teaching about Christ ends with an appeal, and each warning gives way to hope.

Keep an Old Testament close by. Almost every argument in Hebrews rests on a passage of Scripture: Psalm 2, Psalm 8, Psalm 95, Psalm 110, Jeremiah 31, Leviticus 16, Genesis 14. Look them up and the letter opens. Notice the word “better”: a better hope, a better covenant, better promises, better sacrifices, a better country, a better resurrection. Notice how often the author says “let us”, joining his hearers rather than standing over them. And notice the word “Today”, which he means for whoever is reading.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Hebrews are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Apart from God” in 2:9. Almost all manuscripts, including the oldest, say that Jesus tasted death for everyone “by the grace of God”. A very few, known to Origen and other early writers, read “apart from God”, two Greek words that look much alike. The Greek text this translation follows prints the rarer reading, and the translation does the same, with a note giving the other.

“For a little while.” Psalm 8, quoted in 2:7, says God made human beings “a little lower than the angels”. When the author applies it to Jesus in 2:9, the translation reads the same Greek words as time rather than degree: “For a little while he was placed lower than the angels”, in his earthly life and death, and is now crowned.

“Pioneer.” In 2:10 and 12:2 Jesus is “the pioneer”, the one who goes first and leads others after him, where older Bibles have “captain” or “author”.

Covenant and will. The Greek word for covenant can also mean a last will and testament, and in 9:16–17 the author plays on both senses. The translation says “a will” there, and “covenant” everywhere else, so the change of sense can be seen.

“Brothers and sisters.” Where the author addresses his hearers, or speaks of those Jesus is not ashamed to call his own, the Greek word for brothers is rendered “brothers and sisters”, since the whole congregation is meant.

“Christ.” The Open Word Bible lets a reader choose whether Christos reads “Christ” or “the Messiah”. This edition prints “Christ”, but in a letter so full of Israel’s hopes it is worth remembering that the word means God’s anointed King.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Hebrews 1
fields.body_html:
God has spoken by the Son

Long ago God spoke to the ancestors through the prophets, in many separate portions and by many different means. But at the end of these days he has spoken to us through the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things and through whom he also made the ages. The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact stamp of his being, and he bears all things along by his word of power. Having made cleansing for sins through himself, he took his seat at the right hand of the Majesty on high. So he has become far better than the angels, as far as the name that is his by inheritance excels theirs.

The Son is greater than the angels

For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son; this very day I have fathered you”? Or again, “I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to me”? And again, at the time God brings his firstborn into the world, he says, “All the angels of God are to worship him.” About the angels he says, “He turns his angels into winds, and those who serve him into a flame of fire.” But to the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, lasts forever and ever, and the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness. For that reason God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of rejoicing and set you above your companions.” And it also says, “Lord, at the beginning you founded the earth, and the heavens are what your hands have made. They will pass away, but you will remain. All of them will wear out as clothing does; you will fold them up like a cloak, and like clothing they will be replaced. But you are always the same, and your years will have no end.” Has God ever said to any of the angels, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet as a footstool”? Are not all the angels spirits in holy service, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?
fields.summary: God, who spoke long ago through the prophets, has now spoken by the Son, the radiance of God’s glory, who made purification for sins. The Son is far greater than the angels, as the Scriptures show.

fields.title: Hebrews 2
fields.body_html:
Do not drift away

This is why we must give even greater attention to the things we have heard, so that we do not drift off. For if the word that was spoken through angels held good, and every breach of it and every refusal to listen met with the penalty it deserved, how will we escape if we pay no attention to a salvation as great as this? The Lord was the first to speak of it, and it was made certain to us by those who had listened to him, while God added his own testimony by signs and wonders, by many kinds of mighty works, and by sharing out the Holy Spirit as he chose. For God did not place the world to come, the world we are talking about, under the rule of angels. But there is a place where someone has testified, “What is a human being, that you remember him, or a mortal, that you watch over him? You made him a little lower than the angels; with glory and honor you crowned him, and you put all things in subjection under his feet.” When God subjected all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. But as it is, we do not yet see all things put under him. But Jesus we do see. For a little while he was placed lower than the angels, and because of the death he suffered he has been crowned with glory and honor, so that apart from God he should taste death on behalf of everyone.

The pioneer who leads many to glory

For God, for whose sake everything exists and through whom everything exists, was bringing many children to glory, and so it was right for him to bring to perfection through sufferings the pioneer who leads them to salvation. For the one who makes holy and those who are being made holy all come from one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters. He says, “I will make your name known to my brothers and sisters; in the middle of the assembly I will sing your praise.” And again, “I will go on trusting in him.” And again, “Here I am, with the children God has given me.”

Made like us in every way

Since the children, then, share a common life of flesh and blood, he himself took on that same life in the same way, so that by his death he might strip of power the one who holds the power of death, the devil, and release those whom the fear of death kept enslaved their whole life long. For it is clear that he does not take hold of angels to help them; it is Abraham’s descendants that he takes hold of. That is why it was necessary for him to become like his brothers and sisters in every way, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in all that has to do with God, making atonement for the sins of the people. Having suffered himself in being tested, he is able to come to the aid of those who are being tested.
fields.summary: Hearers must not drift away from so great a salvation. Jesus, made lower than the angels for a little while, is the pioneer who leads many to glory, made like us in every way to become a merciful high priest.

fields.title: Hebrews 3
fields.body_html:
Faithful over God’s house

So then, holy brothers and sisters, partners in a heavenly calling, turn your minds to Jesus, the apostle and high priest of the confession we make. He was faithful to God, who appointed him, as Moses too was faithful in God’s house. For Jesus has been judged worthy of more glory than Moses, as surely as the builder of a house is given more honor than the building. Every house, after all, has someone who built it; and the one who built everything is God. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, bearing witness to what God would speak in days to come. But Christ is faithful as the Son, set over God’s house. And we are that house, if we keep hold of our confidence and of the hope we take pride in.

Today, if you hear his voice

So, as the Holy Spirit says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as happened in the rebellion, on that day of testing in the wilderness, where your ancestors put me to the test and tried me, and saw my works for forty years. That is why I was angry with this generation, and I said, ‘Their hearts are forever wandering; they have never come to know my ways.’ So in my anger I swore an oath: ‘They will never enter my rest.’” Watch out, brothers and sisters, so that none of you has a wicked heart that refuses to believe and turns away from the living God. Instead, encourage one another day by day, while there is still a “Today,” so that sin does not deceive any of you and make you hard. For we have become partners of Christ, provided that we keep the confidence we had at the start firm and steady to the very end. As Scripture says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as happened in the rebellion.” Who were the people who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not every one of those who came out of Egypt with Moses as their leader? And who was it that God was angry with for forty years? Was it not the people who had sinned, and whose corpses lay fallen in the wilderness? And who did God swear would never enter his rest, if not those who refused to obey? So we see that it was unbelief that kept them from entering.
fields.summary: Jesus is faithful over God’s house as a son, greater than Moses, who was faithful as a servant. The wilderness generation hardened their hearts and did not enter God’s rest, so hearers must not harden theirs today.

fields.title: Hebrews 4
fields.body_html:
The rest that remains for God’s people

So, while the promise that we may enter his rest is still open, let us be afraid that any one of you might be found to have missed it. For we too have been told good news, as they were. But the message they heard did them no good, because they did not join in faith with those who truly listened. For it is we who have believed who enter that rest, just as he has said, “So in my anger I swore an oath: ‘They will never enter my rest.’” Yet his works had been finished since the world was founded. For somewhere he has spoken of the seventh day in these words: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” And in this passage again: “They will never enter my rest.” So it is still left for some to enter that rest, and those who first heard the good news did not go in, because they would not obey. For this reason God again marks out a certain day, “Today,” speaking through David so long afterward, as was said above: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” If Joshua had brought them into rest, God would not afterward speak of a different day. So a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God’s people. For whoever has entered God’s rest has come to rest from their own works too, just as God did from his. So let us make it our urgent aim to enter that rest, so that no one falls into the same pattern of disobedience.

For the word of God is alive and at work, and it has a keener edge than any two-edged sword. It reaches right in, cutting through soul and spirit, through joints and marrow, and it weighs the thoughts and purposes of the heart. No created thing is concealed from him. All things are stripped bare and open to the eyes of the one we must answer to.

Jesus, the great high priest

We have, then, a great high priest who has gone through the heavens: Jesus the Son of God. So let us keep a firm grip on the confession we make. For the high priest we have is not one who cannot share the feeling of our weaknesses; he has been put to the test in every way, as we are, but without sinning. So let us, with confidence, approach the throne of grace, to receive mercy and to find grace that brings help just when we need it.
fields.summary: A Sabbath rest remains for God’s people, and they must strive to enter it, for God’s word is living and active. Since Jesus is the great high priest who sympathizes with our weakness, we can approach the throne of grace with confidence.

fields.title: Hebrews 5
fields.body_html:
Every high priest is taken from among human beings and put in office on behalf of human beings to deal with what concerns God: he brings gifts and sacrifices for sins. He is able to be gentle and restrained with those who sin in ignorance and wander from the way, since weakness clings to him as well. That weakness is why he must bring offerings for sins on his own account, just as he does for the people. Nobody seizes this honor for himself; it belongs to the one God calls, as God called Aaron.

In the same way Christ did not give himself the glory of becoming high priest. That glory came from the one who said to him, “You are my Son; today I have fathered you.” As he also says in another place, “You are a priest forever, of the order of Melchizedek.” In the days of his life in the flesh, he offered up prayers and pleas, crying aloud and weeping, to the one who was able to save him out of death, and he was heard for his godly fear. Even though he was a Son, he learned obedience by the things he suffered. And having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for everyone who obeys him, for God declared him a high priest of the order of Melchizedek.

From milk to solid food

About this we have a great deal to say, and it is hard to put into words, because you have become sluggish listeners. Given the time that has passed, you ought to be teachers by now; yet once more you need someone to teach you the most basic elements of God’s oracles. You have become people who need milk rather than solid food. Whoever feeds on milk has no experience in the word of righteousness; that person is still an infant. Solid food, on the other hand, belongs to the mature, whose faculties have been trained by practice to tell good from evil.
fields.summary: Every high priest is chosen from among people, and Jesus was appointed by God, a priest in the order of Melchizedek, who learned obedience through suffering. The hearers are slow to learn and still need milk instead of solid food.

fields.title: Hebrews 6
fields.body_html:
So let us leave behind the first message about Christ and be carried forward to maturity. Let us not be laying a foundation all over again: turning away from dead works and putting faith in God, teaching about ritual washings and the laying on of hands, the raising of the dead and eternal judgment. And we will do so, if God allows.

There are those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the gift from heaven, who have received a share in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted that God’s word is good and have tasted the powers of the coming age, and who have then fallen away. It is impossible for them to be brought back again to repentance, as they crucify the Son of God over again for themselves and put him to open shame. When the ground drinks in the rain that falls on it again and again and yields plants that serve the people who work it, it shares in God’s blessing. But if it brings up thorns and thistles, it is rejected as worthless and a curse is close at hand; it will finish by being burned.

Yet about you, dear friends, we are confident of better things, things that come with salvation, even if we talk this way. For God is not so unfair as to forget your work and the love you have shown for his name by serving his holy people, and by serving them still. Our desire is that each of you show the same eagerness right to the end, until your hope is fully assured. Then you will not grow sluggish; you will follow the example of those who, by faith and patience, are receiving the promises as their inheritance.

God’s promise and God’s oath

God made a promise to Abraham, and having no one greater to swear by, he took an oath by himself, saying, “Truly I will bless you richly and multiply you greatly.” And so, after waiting with patience, Abraham obtained the promise. Human beings swear by one greater than they are, and for them an oath settles every dispute, because it confirms what is said. So God, wanting the heirs of the promise to see all the more clearly that his purpose would never change, added an oath to guarantee it. He did this so that through two things that cannot change, and in which God cannot possibly lie, we who have fled for refuge would have strong encouragement to seize the hope placed before us. This hope is ours as an anchor for the soul, one that holds safe and firm and reaches into the inner place behind the curtain. There Jesus entered ahead of us and for our sake, as a forerunner, having become a high priest forever, of the order of Melchizedek.
fields.summary: The writer urges them to go on to maturity, warning of the danger of falling away. God’s promise to Abraham, confirmed by an oath, is an anchor for the soul.

fields.title: Hebrews 7
fields.body_html:
Melchizedek, king and priest

This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham, who was coming back from defeating the kings, and blessed him, and Abraham set aside for him a tenth of everything. Translated, his name means first of all “king of righteousness”; and he is also king of Salem, which means “king of peace.” He is without father, without mother, without genealogy, with no beginning of days and no end of life. Made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time.

See how great this man was: Abraham the patriarch himself gave him a tenth of the choicest plunder. Now those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office are commanded by the law to collect a tenth from the people, that is, from their fellow Israelites, though they too are descended from Abraham. But this man, whose descent is not traced from Levi, took a tenth from Abraham and blessed the man who held the promises. No one can dispute that it is the greater who blesses the lesser. In the one case, the tenth is collected by mortal men; in the other, by one of whom Scripture testifies that he lives. One might even say that Levi, who receives the tenth, paid the tenth through Abraham, for Levi was still in the body of his ancestor when Melchizedek met Abraham.

A different priest and a better hope

If the Levitical priesthood could have brought perfection (and the people’s law was given on the basis of that priesthood), why would a different priest still have to arise, a priest of the order of Melchizedek, and not one named of the order of Aaron? A change of priesthood necessarily brings with it a change of law. The one of whom these things are said belongs to a different tribe, and no one from that tribe has ever served at the altar. It is plain to all that our Lord came from Judah, and Moses said nothing at all about priests from that tribe.

And this becomes clearer still, since another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, one who has become a priest not by a legal rule about bodily descent but by the power of a life that cannot be destroyed. For Scripture testifies of him, “You are a priest forever of the order of Melchizedek.” So the commandment that came before is annulled, for it was weak and could not help, since the law brought nothing to perfection. Instead a better hope has been brought in, and by that hope we come near to God.

And this was done with an oath. The others became priests with no oath, but he became a priest with an oath, sworn by the one who said to him, “The Lord has sworn, and he will not go back on it: ‘You are a priest forever.’” As much greater as that oath makes his priesthood, so much better is the covenant of which Jesus has become the guarantee.

There have been many Levitical priests, one after another, because death cut short each one’s service; But he remains forever, and so the priesthood he holds will never pass to another. For this reason he is able to save completely those who approach God through him, since he is always alive to plead on their behalf.

This is the kind of high priest that suits our need: holy, innocent, unstained, separate from sinners, and raised above the heavens. He has no need to do what the other high priests do day by day: offer sacrifices first for their own sins and then for the sins of the people. He did that once for all when he offered up himself. The law appoints mortal men, weak as they are, to be high priests. But the oath, sworn later than the law, appoints a Son, made perfect forever.
fields.summary: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, was greater than Abraham and Levi. Jesus is a different priest who lives forever, bringing a better hope than the law could.

fields.title: Hebrews 8
fields.body_html:
The high priest of a new covenant

Here is the heart of what we are saying. Our high priest is one who has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and he serves in the sanctuary, the true tabernacle, pitched by the Lord and not by a human being. The task of every high priest is to present gifts and sacrifices, so our high priest too must have something to present. On earth he would not even be a priest, for there are already men who present the gifts the law requires. The worship they offer is service in a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. So when Moses was about to set up the tabernacle, God instructed him: “Take care,” he said, “to make everything according to the pattern you were shown on the mountain.” As it is, he has been given a far higher ministry, in keeping with the better covenant of which he is mediator, a covenant set in law on better promises.

Had that first covenant been free of fault, no room would have been sought for a second one. For God finds fault with them when he says, “A time is coming, says the Lord, when I will bring about a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. It will differ from the covenant I made with their ancestors on the day I took hold of their hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. They did not hold to my covenant, so I paid them no more attention, says the Lord.” “For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel when those days are past, says the Lord: I will place my laws in their understanding and inscribe them on their hearts. I will be God to them, and they will be a people to me.” “None of them will need to teach a fellow citizen or a brother or sister, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all of them will know me, from the least to the greatest.” “For I will show mercy to their wrongdoing, and their sins I will never again call to mind.” By calling the covenant “new,” he has treated the first as old, and what grows old and worn out is close to vanishing.
fields.summary: Jesus is the high priest who serves in the true tabernacle in heaven. Jesus mediates a new covenant, the one God promised through the prophets, which makes the first one obsolete.

fields.title: Hebrews 9
fields.body_html:
Worship in the earthly tabernacle

The first covenant, then, had its own regulations for worship, and a sanctuary belonging to this world. A first tabernacle was set up, which held the lampstand, and the table with the loaves set out on it. This one is called the Holy Place. Beyond the second curtain stood a tabernacle called the Most Holy Place. To it belonged the golden altar of incense, and in it was the ark of the covenant, overlaid with gold on every side. The ark held a golden jar containing the manna, the staff of Aaron that sprouted, and the tablets of the covenant. Over the ark the cherubim of glory spread their shadow across the mercy seat. Of these things there is no time now to speak one by one.

With these things arranged in this way, the priests go regularly into the first tabernacle as they carry out their duties of worship. But into the second the high priest goes alone, once a year, and he must bring blood, which he offers for his own sins and for those the people committed without knowing it. By this the Holy Spirit makes it clear that the way into the sanctuary has not yet been opened as long as the first tabernacle still has its place. This is a figure for the present time. Under this arrangement gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot make the worshiper perfect in conscience. They have to do only with what is eaten and drunk and with various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time comes to set things right. But Christ came as high priest of the good things that have now come. Through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, one not made by hands and not belonging to this creation, and by means not of the blood of goats and calves but of his own blood, he entered the sanctuary once for all and obtained an eternal redemption. For if the blood of goats and bulls, and a heifer’s ashes sprinkled on people who have become defiled, make them holy so that they are clean in body, how much more will the blood of Christ wash our conscience clean of dead works, so that we may worship the living God! Through the eternal Spirit he offered himself to God, a sacrifice without flaw.

This is why he mediates a new covenant: a death has taken place to set people free from the offenses committed under the first covenant, and so those who are called may receive what was promised, the eternal inheritance. A will, after all, requires proof that the one who made it has died. For it is when someone has died that a will becomes binding; it has no force at all as long as its maker is alive. This is why not even the first covenant was dedicated apart from blood. Moses first spoke every command of the law to all the people. Then he took the calves’ blood together with water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled the book itself and the whole people, and said, “This is the blood of the covenant God has laid down for you.” Likewise he sprinkled blood on the tabernacle as well, and on all the vessels used in its worship. The law, in fact, has almost everything made clean with blood, and where no blood is shed there is no forgiveness.

Into heaven itself

The copies of what is in heaven, then, had to be cleansed in these ways; but the heavenly realities themselves required sacrifices better than these. For it was not into a sanctuary made by hands, a copy of the real one, that Christ went. He went into heaven itself, and there he now appears before the face of God on our behalf. And he did not enter to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest goes into the sanctuary each year with blood that belongs to another. If that were so, he would have needed to suffer many times over, ever since the world was founded. Instead, he has now been revealed once, when the ages reach their completion, to set sin aside through his sacrifice. And as it is in store for human beings to die once and after that to be judged, so Christ too was offered once to carry the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, apart from sin, to those who eagerly await him for their salvation.
fields.summary: Under the first covenant priests entered the earthly tabernacle with the blood of animals. Jesus entered heaven itself, not with the blood of animals but by a single offering made once for all, to secure eternal redemption.

fields.title: Hebrews 10
fields.body_html:
One sacrifice, once for all

For the law holds only a shadow of the good things to come, not the very form of the things themselves. It can never, by the same sacrifices offered without end each year, make perfect those who approach. Otherwise, would the offerings not have come to an end? The worshipers, once cleansed, would no longer carry sins on their conscience. Instead, these sacrifices bring sins back to mind every year, because the blood of bulls and goats cannot take sins away. That is why, as Christ comes into the world, he says: “Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but a body you have made ready for me.” “In burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no delight.” “Then I said, ‘See, O God, I have come to do your will, just as the scroll of the book says of me.’” First he says, “Sacrifices and offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings you did not want and took no delight in”, though these are the offerings the law prescribes. Then he says, “See, I have come to do your will.” He removes the first in order to put the second in its place. It is by that will that we have been made holy, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ, made once for all.

Every priest stands at his duties day after day, offering over and over the same sacrifices, and these can never remove sins. This priest, though, offered a single sacrifice for sins, good for all time, and then sat down at the right hand of God. From then on he is waiting for his enemies to be put under his feet as a footstool. By that one offering he has brought those who are being made holy to perfection for all time. The Holy Spirit also bears witness to this for us. For after first saying, “This is the covenant I will establish with them when those days are past, says the Lord: I will set my laws on their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.” Then he adds, “Their sins and their acts of lawlessness I will not call to mind ever again.” And once these have been forgiven, no further offering for sin remains to be made.

Let us approach God with confidence

So then, brothers and sisters, the blood of Jesus has given us confidence to go into the sanctuary. He has opened for us a way that is new and living, a way through the curtain, which is his flesh. And we have a great priest who is over the house of God. So let us approach with hearts that are true, fully sure in our faith, our hearts sprinkled and cleansed of an evil conscience and our bodies bathed in clean water. Let us cling to the confession of our hope without bending, for the one who made the promise is faithful. Let us also keep one another in mind, so as to rouse each other to love and good works. Let us not walk away from our own gatherings, as some have made it their practice, but keep urging one another on, and do it more and more as you see the day coming closer.

A warning against deliberate sin

If we keep on sinning on purpose after we have come to know the truth, there is no sacrifice for sins left for us. All that remains is a terrifying prospect of judgment and of a blazing fire that will devour those who oppose God. Whoever disregards Moses’ law is put to death without pity, if two or three witnesses testify. How much worse, then, do you think is the punishment deserved by someone who has trampled on the Son of God, counted as ordinary the blood of the covenant that made such a person holy, and treated the Spirit of grace with contempt? For we know the one who said, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will pay it back,” and who also said, “The Lord will judge his people.” Falling into the hands of the living God is a terrifying thing.

Do not throw away your confidence

Think back to those earlier days, after you had been enlightened, when you endured a hard contest of suffering. At times you were mocked and mistreated in front of everyone; at other times you shared the lot of those who were treated like that. You shared in the suffering of those in prison, and when your goods were seized you welcomed it with joy, for you knew that you owned something better, something that lasts. So do not let go of your confidence; a great reward comes with it. What you need is endurance, so that once you have done God’s will you may obtain the promise. For, “In a very short while now, the one who is coming will arrive and will not be slow in coming.” “But my righteous one will live by faith; and if he turns back, my soul finds no delight in him.” But we are not people who draw back and are lost; we are people of faith, and our lives will be kept safe.
fields.summary: The law’s sacrifices could never take away sins, but Jesus offered one sacrifice for sins, once for all. So believers can approach God with confidence and hold fast to their hope; deliberate sin is warned against, and they must not throw away their confidence.

fields.title: Hebrews 11
fields.body_html:
What faith is

Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for, the proof of realities we do not see. This is how the people of long ago gained God’s approval. By faith we understand that the ages were set in order by God’s word, so that what we see did not come into being from anything visible.

By faith Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain’s. Through faith he was attested as righteous, since God bore witness about his gifts. And through faith, though he died, he is still speaking.

By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death; he could not be found, because God had taken him away. Before he was taken, it was attested of him that he had pleased God. And no one can please God without faith, since anyone who approaches God has to believe both that he exists and that he repays those who search for him. By faith Noah, warned by God about what could not yet be seen, acted with reverence and built an ark for the salvation of his household. Through this he passed sentence on the world, and he came to inherit the righteousness that faith brings.

The faith of Abraham

By faith Abraham obeyed God’s call to leave for a land he would later be given as his own, and he set out without knowing where he was headed. By faith he lived as a resident alien in the land of the promise, as if it were someone else’s country. He lived in tents, along with Isaac and Jacob, his fellow heirs of that same promise. For he was waiting for the city with firm foundations, a city planned and built by God. By faith, together with Sarah herself, he received the power to become a father, even though he was past the age for it, since he held that the one who had made the promise was faithful. So it was that from one man, whose body was already as if dead, there came descendants as many as the stars of heaven, as numberless as the sand along the shore of the sea.

All these died still holding to faith. They did not receive what was promised, but they saw it from far off and welcomed it, and they openly said that they were foreigners and passing visitors on the earth. Those who talk this way are showing that they are in search of a homeland. Had their minds been on the land they came out of, they would have had time enough to turn back. But as things are, they are reaching out for something better: a homeland in heaven. So God does not count it a shame to be known as their God, and he has made a city ready for them.

By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac. The man who had been given the promises was offering up his only son, the son about whom he had been told, “Your offspring will be named through Isaac.” He counted on God’s power to raise people even from the dead, and from the dead, in a figure, he did receive him back.

By faith Isaac also blessed Jacob and Esau with regard to what was still to come. By faith Jacob, at the point of death, blessed each of Joseph’s sons, and he bowed low in worship over the tip of his staff. By faith Joseph, when his life was coming to an end, spoke of the Israelites’ coming exodus and gave orders about his bones.

The faith of Moses

By faith, when Moses was born, his parents kept him hidden for three months. They saw what a fine child he was, and they did not fear the king’s decree. By faith Moses, once he was a grown man, would not let himself be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. He chose to share the hardships of God’s people instead of enjoying sin’s pleasures for a short time. He reckoned that to bear the reproach of Christ was worth more than all the riches of Egypt, because he kept his eyes on the reward. By faith he left Egypt, unafraid of the king’s rage, and he held firm as one who saw the unseen God. By faith he held the Passover and had the blood spread on the doorframes, so that the one who struck down the firstborn would not touch the Israelites.

By faith Israel went through the Red Sea as if it were dry ground; the Egyptians made the attempt too, and the sea swallowed them. By faith the walls of Jericho fell, when Israel had gone around them day after day for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute escaped the death of those who refused to obey, since she had taken in the spies in peace.

More witnesses of faith

And what more should I say? Time would run out on me if I told about Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah, about David and Samuel and the prophets. Through faith they overcame kingdoms, ruled with justice, won what had been promised, and shut the mouths of lions. They put out the power of fire, got away from the sword’s edge, found strength when they were weak, grew mighty in war, and drove back foreign armies. Women had their dead given back to them, raised to life. Others were tortured and beaten, and they would not accept freedom, because they wanted to obtain a better resurrection. Others went through mockery and the lash, and beyond that, chains and prison cells. They were stoned, sawn in two, cut down by the sword. They roamed about wearing the skins of sheep and goats, lacking everything, oppressed, treated cruelly. The world did not deserve such people. They wandered over deserts and mountains, and sheltered in caves and in holes in the earth. Through their faith all of these were attested by God, and yet they did not receive the promise. God had in view something better for us: they were not to be made perfect apart from us.
fields.summary: Faith is the assurance of what is hoped for. The writer recalls the faith of Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses and many more witnesses, who did not receive what was promised.

fields.title: Hebrews 12
fields.body_html:
Running with our eyes on Jesus

So then, since we too have so vast a cloud of witnesses all around us, let us strip off every burden, and the sin that wraps itself around us so readily, and let us run the race laid out ahead of us, and run it with endurance. Let us keep our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer who leads the way in faith and brings it to perfection. For the sake of the joy that lay ahead of him, he endured a cross and counted its shame as nothing, and he has taken his seat at the right hand of God’s throne.

God disciplines his children

Weigh up what he endured: such hostility from sinners, who were really working against themselves. Then you will not wear out and let your spirits give way. Your fight against sin has not yet cost you your blood. And you have forgotten the encouraging word that speaks to you as children: “My son, do not shrug off the Lord’s discipline, and do not give way when he corrects you. Those whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and he brings the whip down on every son he takes as his own.” What you endure, you endure as discipline. God is dealing with you as children; and what child is there that a father does not discipline? If you go without the discipline that all children share in, then you are illegitimate, not true children. Again: our human fathers corrected us, and we held them in respect. Should we not much more put ourselves under the Father of spirits, and so live? Those fathers disciplined us for a short span of years, in whatever way seemed right to them. God does it for what truly benefits us, so that we may come to share in his holiness. At the time it is given, no discipline seems a matter for joy; it seems a matter for sorrow. But afterward it pays back those who have been trained by it with a harvest of peace: righteousness.

So raise your tired hands again and steady your shaking knees. Make the tracks your feet walk on straight, so that the limb that is lame is not wrenched out of joint, but is healed instead.

Pursue peace and holiness

Seek peace with everyone, and go after holiness, since apart from it no one will see the Lord. Watch over one another, so that none of you comes short of God’s grace, no bitter root shoots up and causes trouble, defiling many through it, and no one is sexually immoral or without regard for what is holy, as Esau was. He gave up his rights as the firstborn in exchange for one meal. You know that later, when he wanted to receive the blessing as his inheritance, he was turned away. He found no opening for repentance, even though he begged for it with tears.

Mount Sinai and Mount Zion

You have not approached a mountain that could be touched, ablaze with fire, nor darkness and gloom and storm, nor the blast of a trumpet and a voice speaking, so that those who heard it begged not to be spoken to anymore. The order was more than they could bear: “Even an animal that touches the mountain must be stoned.” What appeared was so fearsome that Moses said, “I am full of dread, and I am shaking.” No: you have approached Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have approached myriads of angels, a festival gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. You have approached a judge who is God of all, and the spirits of righteous people who have been made perfect, and Jesus, mediator of a new covenant, and blood sprinkled for cleansing, which says something better than Abel said.

Do not refuse the one who speaks

Be careful not to refuse the one who is speaking to you. They rejected the one who warned them on earth, and they did not escape. Far less will we escape if we turn our backs on the one who warns us from heaven. At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has made a promise: “One more time I will shake not the earth alone, but heaven as well.” That phrase, “one more time,” makes clear that whatever is shaken will be removed, since it belongs to what was made, so that what is not shaken will remain. So, as people who are being given a kingdom that nothing can shake, let us hold on to gratitude, and through it serve God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe. For our God really is a consuming fire.
fields.summary: Surrounded by these witnesses, believers are to run with their eyes on Jesus, accepting hardship as God’s discipline of children. They have come not to Mount Sinai but to Mount Zion, and must not refuse the one who speaks.

fields.title: Hebrews 13
fields.body_html:
Keep loving one another

Let your love for one another as brothers and sisters remain. Do not forget to open your homes to strangers. By doing this, some people have had angels as their guests and never knew it. Keep in mind those in prison, as if you were in chains alongside them, and those who are being ill-treated, since you also live in a body. All of you should treat marriage as precious and keep the marriage bed undefiled; God will judge those who are sexually immoral and those who are unfaithful in marriage. Do not let love of money rule the way you live; be satisfied with what you have. For God himself has said, “I will not ever let you go, and I will never, never abandon you.” That is why we can say boldly, “The Lord is the one who helps me; I will have no fear. What can any human being do to me?” Keep in mind those who led you, who brought you the word of God. Look closely at where their way of life led them, and follow the example of their faith. Yesterday and today, Jesus Christ is the same, and so he will be for all the ages. Do not let all kinds of unfamiliar teachings sweep you off course. It is good for the heart to be made firm by grace, not by foods; those who have lived by them have gained nothing. There is an altar that is ours, and those who carry out the service of the tabernacle are not allowed to eat from it. When animals are offered for sin, the high priest takes their blood into the sanctuary, and their bodies are burned outside the camp. That is why Jesus, too, suffered outside the gate: so that by his own blood he might make the people holy. So let us go out to him, outside the camp, and share the insults heaped on him. There is no city here that remains for us; the city we are looking for is the one still to come. So through him let us offer God a sacrifice of praise at all times: the fruit of lips that give thanks to his name. And do not forget to be kind and to share with one another: God delights in sacrifices of this kind.

Leaders, and a request for prayer

Follow your leaders and yield to them. They stay awake watching over your souls, as people who will have to answer for them. Make it possible for them to do this with joy instead of sighing, since that would bring you no gain.

Keep praying for us. We are confident that our conscience is good, since we want to live rightly in every way. And I ask you even more earnestly to do this, so that I may be brought back to you all the sooner.

A closing blessing

May the God of peace, who led our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, up from the dead through the blood of an eternal covenant, make you ready in every good thing for doing his will. May he bring about in us whatever pleases him, through Jesus Christ. To him be the glory for all the ages. Amen.

Final words

Brothers and sisters, I urge you to put up with this message of encouragement; after all, I have written you only a short letter. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released. If he gets here soon enough, he will be with me when I see you. Greet all your leaders and all God’s holy people. Those from Italy send you their greetings. Grace be with all of you.
fields.summary: Believers are to keep loving one another, show hospitality and remember prisoners, and to obey their leaders. The letter closes with a request for prayer, a blessing and final greetings.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
May the God of peace, who led our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, up from the dead through the blood of an eternal covenant, make you ready in every good thing for doing his will. May he bring about in us whatever pleases him, through Jesus Christ. To him be the glory for all the ages. Amen.

— Hebrews 13:20–21

Hebrews ends with a prayer, and the prayer gathers the whole letter into a single sentence. God has led Jesus up from the dead; Jesus is the great shepherd, as he was the great high priest; the covenant is eternal, and it was made with blood. And after twelve chapters of urging the hearers to hold on, the author asks God to do in them what he has been asking them to do. The God who calls them to endure is the God who will make them ready.

Then, with a touch of humour, he asks them to bear with his “short letter”, sends news of Timothy, and is gone.

The question the letter leaves

Hebrews leaves its readers with one question, asked in many forms: will you keep going? Its first hearers were not wondering whether Jesus was real. They had believed, suffered for it, and seen their goods taken. What they faced was the slow pull of weariness, the habit of missing the gatherings, the thought that the old, familiar ways had been safer. The author never answers that weariness by scolding alone. He answers it by showing them Jesus, again and again, until the question becomes: having seen him, where else would you go?

That is why the letter keeps returning to the word “Today”. The rest is still open, the throne of grace is still approachable, the voice is still speaking. But it speaks now, and the answer is given now. “Be careful not to refuse the one who is speaking to you.”

Where the letter points

It points forward. Hebrews is full of people who died without receiving what was promised and went on looking for a country of their own. The author counts his readers among them. They have come to Mount Zion already, and yet they are still seeking the city to come. The Christian life, in Hebrews, is a pilgrimage with the destination already in view:

So, as people who are being given a kingdom that nothing can shake, let us hold on to gratitude, and through it serve God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe. For our God really is a consuming fire.

— Hebrews 12:28–29

And it points to one another. The letter that soars into the heavenly sanctuary also tells its readers to keep each other in mind, to rouse each other to love, to open their homes, to visit prisoners, and to go on meeting. Endurance, in Hebrews, is never a solitary virtue. It is something a congregation does together, encouraging one another day by day.

Where to go from here

Hebrews has fed the church’s preaching and prayer for as long as there has been a church, and many of its best interpreters are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • Through the whole letter. F. B. Meyer’s The Way into the Holiest, devotional expositions that follow Hebrews from its first verse to its closing prayer.
  • On Christ the Son (chapter 1). Athanasius of Alexandria’s Against the Arians, which works through Hebrews 1:4 and 3:2 in defending the full divinity of the Son.
  • On the rest that remains (chapters 3–4). Richard Baxter’s The Saints’ Everlasting Rest, his great treatise on 4:9; Charles H. Spurgeon’s sermon Heavenly Rest, on the same verse; and R. A. Torrey’s The Day of Golden Opportunity, on “Today” (3:7).
  • On the high priest who intercedes (chapters 4–7). Spurgeon’s Salvation to the Uttermost and J. C. Ryle’s Christ’s Power to Save in Old Paths, both on 7:25; Andrew Murray’s The School of Obedience, whose chapter The Secret of True Obedience is on 5:8; and Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s So Great Salvation, on the first warning (2:1–4).
  • On the new covenant and the open way (chapters 8–10). Andrew Murray’s The Two Covenants; Horatius Bonar’s The Rent Veil, on the curtain torn open; and A. W. Tozer’s The Pursuit of God, whose chapter Removing the Veil is on 10:19.
  • On faith (chapter 11). Spurgeon’s Faith (11:6); John Wesley’s sermons On Faith and On the Discoveries of Faith (11:1), in Sermons on Several Occasions; and Jonathan Edwards’s The Christian Pilgrim (11:13–14).
  • On the race and the mountain (chapter 12). A. B. Simpson’s The Cloud of Witnesses (12:1), The School of Faith (12:11) and The Goal of Faith (12:18–24); Spurgeon’s The Shameful Sufferer (12:2); J. C. Ryle’s Holiness, whose title chapter is on 12:14; and George MacDonald’s The Consuming Fire (12:29), in Unspoken Sermons.
  • Outside the camp (chapter 13). John Calvin’s Enduring Persecution for Christ (13:13) and Spurgeon’s The Blood of the Everlasting Covenant, on the closing prayer (13:20).

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Hebrews in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read Hebrews again, slowly this time, with its Old Testament passages open beside it. And when the weariness it was written for comes, as it comes to everyone, remember the one sentence the letter wants you never to forget:

Yesterday and today, Jesus Christ is the same, and so he will be for all the ages.

— Hebrews 13:8
